newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch investigate metals investment company.
newsitem.headline: Dutch investigate metals investment company.

text.p: Dutch finance officials said on Thursday they were investigating an Amsterdam-based company over the sale of titanium for investment.
"We have been investigating the company on possible investment fraud," an official at the Economische Controle Dienst (ECD) told Reuters.
The ECD, part of the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs, said it was investigating Avington International Ltd for possible breaches of Dutch securities law.
The official, who declined to be named, gave no further details and attempts by Reuters to contact Avington have so far been unsuccessful.
Asked if Avington employees were still at its Amsterdam address, the ECD official, said: "No, the offices are empty and we are searching for them."
An ECD spokesman urged anyone who had invested in titanium through Avington to contact their local police.

"We're trying to find out what they were doing, if they were operating within Dutch securities rules. They were offering the possibility to buy titanium and in some instances you need a licence for that," he said.
Avington apparently offered investors the chance to buy into the metal, prized for its high strength-to-mass ratio and widely used in aerospace.

The company deposited titanium on behalf of investors at a Rotterdam warehouse owned by Racon Ocean, which is not under investigation, and sent letters to clients two weeks ago telling them to claim their metal.

"Technically our investigation ended when they (Avington) finished their activities but we have a responsibility to foreign law enforcement bodies," the ECD spokesman said. "A lot of Avington clients have contacted us and they feel defrauded. They think they might not get their money back or their titanium."
Racon managing director Leen Lok told Reuters he thought he had spotted irregularities in Avington's paper work and called in the ECD to check.
He said there seemed to be more than 150 clients around the world who had bought titanium by the kilo between July 1996 and February this year.
Some invoices, however, suggested an unusually high price had been paid, according to Lok. He declined to say how much metal Racon was holding.
